title: The Two Empty Boxes in the Bottom-Right Corner of the Map
teaser: Only ten days remain before the open day, and heavy rain has turned the public garden’s children’s path into a shallow channel. Two drainage plans, the materials, and the construction method are already prepared. The engineering volunteer asks only that two site conditions be confirmed before work begins, yet three people still cannot put one shared line on the same map and act on it.
paragraphs: Ten days remain before the open day, but the previous night’s rain has cut off the children’s path through the public garden. Cheng Yue spreads the two drainage plans left by the engineering volunteer across a bench. Both meet the basic slope and safety requirements, and the gravel, drainage channel, and tools have already arrived. In the bottom-right corner of the drawing are only two small boxes to be confirmed before construction: the actual position of the main root, and the main point where rainwater enters. Old Zhou worries that the shorter trench will damage the pear tree, more than twenty years old. He Qing worries that if they swing too far around the roots, the next rain will close the path again. Cheng Yue worries most that the path will still be shut ten days from now. All three concerns are reasonable. The two boxes remain empty.

At their first meeting, Cheng Yue starts by fixing the dates: trench on Saturday, gravel on Sunday, path reopened on Monday. Old Zhou agrees to help with the work but shifts the short-trench line farther away from the tree. He Qing also accepts the schedule, then pulls the drainage line back toward the low edge of the bricks. All three explain their reasons clearly, and no one refuses to cooperate. Cheng Yue reads through the engineering notes again and confirms that either design can be implemented after the site checks. By sunset, several pencil lines on the map have become darker, but the two boxes marked “main root” and “water inflow” still have no ticks.

It rains again the next day. Cheng Yue returns to the site with the map, intending to call the engineering volunteer and ask them to choose between the two plans. Raindrops wrinkle the edge of the paper. She sees the two empty boxes in the bottom-right corner and puts her phone away. For the moment, the three of them leave the design lines alone. Old Zhou and He Qing dig three narrow inspection pits together, while Cheng Yue places wooden markers at both ends of the path and, after the rain eases, follows the retreating water and marks its trace. Old Zhou walks the full line of standing water for the first time; He Qing kneels beside the pear tree and looks at the roots for the first time. None of the checking methods is new. What is new is that, until now, none of them has been willing to set their own preferred line aside first and do the checks together.

The pits show that the main root lies about half a meter away from the position shown on the old plan. The water marks beside the stakes show that most of the runoff enters at the low edge of the bricks. The result does not automatically declare a winner. The short trench is still feasible, and the route around the roots is still feasible; both people’s original risks now have to be included. Old Zhou shifts the short trench outward within the range already allowed by the original plan. He Qing agrees to build the shorter section first and leave a connection at the end so it can be extended later. Cheng Yue ticks the two boxes and draws the revised line and construction order back onto the original map. No extra materials appear, and no miraculous third design is invented.

When construction starts on Saturday, one volunteer who was supposed to carry materials does not turn up, and the work immediately falls two hours behind. If the earlier problem had only been missing site data, it should now be solved. Instead, a new trade-off appears at once: finish the easy decorative edging first, or first secure a safe path, functioning drainage, and permeable soil around the roots. The three do not retreat to defending separate lines again. Old Zhou monitors the digging depth. He Qing temporarily lets go of the full long trench he originally preferred and reorganizes the remaining people to move gravel. Cheng Yue removes the decorative edging from that day’s plan and marks the minimum condition for reopening beside the map.

The day before the open day, the children’s path reopens. The drainage channel passes outside the main root, and the extension connection at its end is still exposed. Cheng Yue carries the garden map back to the activity room. The first two route lines, the rain-blurred crease, the three inspection pits, the two ticks, and the later construction order are all still visible on the paper. She does not copy it onto a clean sheet. She spreads the map flat and places one small stone from the garden on each of its four corners.
concept: The Inner Development Goals (IDG) use dimensions such as Being, Thinking, Relating, Collaborating, and Acting to help understand which inner capacities support complex goals alongside external technology, resources, and institutions. The framework focuses on how people notice their own judgments, work with complexity and uncertainty, understand others, collaborate, and continue acting. IDG is better used as a map for reflection and capability development than as a personality scale that scores individuals item by item.
explanation: The story treats “the technical plans were not good enough” and “people simply failed to communicate clearly” as the strongest alternative explanations and works to exclude them. Both plans are feasible from the beginning, and the engineering notes already specify the two site checks required before construction; the three people have also explained their reasons fully. Progress stalls because each person still treats their own risk judgment as a condition that must first be accepted, so the existing technical tools are not used jointly. The behavioral turn comes when they put ownership of the preferred plan aside, examine uncertainty together, directly encounter the risks the others care about, and revise their own initial judgments accordingly. Later, the missing volunteer creates a new execution constraint. They can still reorder the work around a shared minimum goal, which shows that the change is not merely the addition of one set of rain-day data but a change in how they handle uncertainty, relationships, and joint action.
mapping: Two feasible plans and two site checks exist from the beginning → External technical means are broadly available, so the delay cannot be reduced to “there is no solution”

All three have already explained their reasons, yet the two check boxes remain empty → Information exchange alone is not enough for shared judgment; people must also be willing to examine their own assumptions and enter the risk perspective of others

They dig inspection pits together, follow the retreating water, and each revise part of the position they had defended → Handling complexity, understanding relationships, and collaborating change how the existing technical tools are used

After a volunteer is absent, they can still reorganize around the minimum condition for reopening → Inner capacities affect not only shared understanding but also how the team acts together under a new constraint
boundary: IDG cannot replace engineering design, professional judgment, budgets, institutions, or clear authority. If a plan is unsafe, resources are fundamentally inadequate, or governance conflict blocks action, improving inner capacities alone will not solve the problem. The five dimensions should also not be treated as fixed stages or as a personality scorecard. This story applies only where external conditions are broadly workable but a complex goal still requires people to handle their own judgments, uncertainty, relationships, and collaboration more effectively.
reflection: When feasible plans, tools, and information channels already exist, is the team stuck because it lacks one more answer, or because it lacks the capacity to handle uncertainty together?
